title: POC Weekly Sync - throughput optim
summary: Weekly POC sync to review throughput runs and tune continuous batching, concurrency targets and queueing. SE reviewed test results: baseline hosted run, batching enabled, and queued requests behavior. Action: run longer stress tests, try concurrency 48/96, verify KV cache hit patterns, update benchmark sheet, share recommended config and pricing estimate.
action_items: Samir Patel - run 2h stress with concurrency targets 48 and 96 and attach logs - due 2026-11-22
Marcus Chen - provide mean/95th latency SLOs and current traffic shaping config - due 2026-11-20

meeting_header:
Date: 2026-11-18
Time: 16:00 PT
Duration: 45 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE); Samir Patel (Redwood SE); Aisha Gomez (NimblePay Director of ML); Marcus Chen (NimblePay Infra); Priya Rao (NimblePay PM)
transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Lee: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we'll kick off. Quick agenda: review last week's runs, look at continuous batching changes, and pick concurrency targets.
[00:12] Aisha Gomez: yep thanks, we had a couple infra meetings this morning so should be good.
[00:20] Samir Patel: Alright, I'll share my screen in a sec, but quick TL;DR — baseline hosted run with default batching gave us about 210 qps at 95th latency ~280ms for 512 token requests. Enabling continuous batching bumped effective qps to ~490 but 95th moved up to ~340ms, so tradeoff there.
[00:45] Marcus Chen: sorry can you repeat baseline numbers? I missed the first one.
[00:48] Samir Patel: baseline: 210 queries per second, 95th latency 280ms, mean ~120ms. With continuous batching we get 480-500 qps but 95th around 330-350ms. There's some variance on tail.
[01:05] Aisha Gomez: okay that matches what we saw in our short run friday - interesting. Our user SLO is 300ms 95th ideally, but we can tolerate 400ms during spikes.
[01:18] Jordan Lee: good to call that out — so goal is to hit 300ms 95th under steady load while maximizing tokens/sec. Tradeoffs: batching increases throughput but adds queueing delay which affects tail.
[01:30] Priya Rao: any notes on KV cache hits? last run we saw low hit rates and that might be driving extra compute.
[01:36] Samir Patel: yup good call. On the demo dataset the prefix patterns are diverse, KV hit rate was only about 12% in initial runs. We changed prefixing and saw it jump to 28% in one experiment which helped reduce tokens per request on average. But the production pattern might be less cacheable.
[01:55] Marcus Chen: are those KV hits coming from the same session affinity? our traffic is multi-tenant so affinity's tricky.
[02:02] Samir Patel: it's mixed — session affinity helps a lot. We recommended sticky routing for a subset of customers for POC to see benefits. If affinity is off, caching helps less.
[02:15] Aisha Gomez: for a lot of our conversational flows we do a lot of short context, but we do some long session threads that would benefit. Maybe we can try hybrid — sticky for test users.
[02:28] Jordan Lee: cool. I ran the cost model quickly: at 480 qps hosted with batching, cost per 1M tokens goes down ~18% vs baseline because of better packing, but user-perceived tail latency increases.
[02:42] Priya Rao: what about concurrency targets? Marcus and I debated whether to aim for concurrency of 48 cores per model instance or 96.
[02:50] Samir Patel: here's what we saw in microbenchmarks: single worker throughput scales up to ~64 concurrent requests before diminishing returns; above that kernel scheduling overhead creeps in. But on some GPUs with optimized kernels we saw good scaling to 96. It's model and hardware dependent.
[03:11] Marcus Chen: we're on A100s in prod for this POC, right?
[03:15] Jordan Lee: yes, current POC is on A100s in the hosted pool. For Dedicated we can tune more.
[03:20] Marcus Chen: ok wondering if we should push concurrency to 96 for throughput peak and have autoscaling for tail.
[03:27] Samir Patel: you can, but expect higher variance in tail. One pattern we recommend: target two concurrency profiles — steady-state concurrency 48, burst concurrency 96 with queue-based admission control. That keeps 95th acceptable most of the time and allows bursts to be absorbed with controlled degradation.
[03:46] Aisha Gomez: queue-based admission control? like reject or delay?
[03:49] Samir Patel: delay, backpressure queue that applies prioritization and drop rules. For example, requests older than X ms can be dropped or routed to a cheaper model variant. We can configure per-route queue sizes.
[04:04] Priya Rao: can you show the queueing plots from the run?
[04:07] Samir Patel: sure pulling up the benchmark sheet — bear with me. (sound of mouse) 
[04:18] Samir Patel: okay here's the histogram: when we pushed to concurrency 96 with continuous batching, average queue wait was ~85ms, but 95th queue wait hit 420ms for a subset of requests, which is why 95th latency climbed.
[04:34] Marcus Chen: 420ms just in queue? that seems high.
[04:37] Samir Patel: yep queue + execution. If you reduce concurrency to 48, 95th queue wait drops to ~120ms. Throughput is lower but tail improves.
[04:46] Aisha Gomez: is there a way to keep throughput high and cap queue wait? like hybrid batching threshold?
[04:51] Samir Patel: we do have a batching policy that caps max batch assembly time (max_batch_delay) and also a min tokens threshold. Setting a tighter max_batch_delay reduces queue waits but also reduces batch sizes. Another lever is dynamic batching — adapt batch size to current request rate while enforcing a max hold time.
[05:10] Jordan Lee: Samir mentioned dynamic batching last week, did you try auto-scaling batch time in the sandbox?
[05:15] Samir Patel: yes, in the experimental run I set max_batch_delay to 8ms for low-latency profile and to 25ms for high-throughput. At 8ms we saw batch sizes of ~6 requests with qps ~260, at 25ms batch sizes ~18 with qps ~480. So it's a clear knob.
[05:33] Marcus Chen: hmm for our mix I'd prefer 15ms maybe.
[05:36] Aisha Gomez: agree, 15ms could be a good compromise. What's the work for Samir to run a 2h test with 15ms and concurrency step test?
[05:45] Samir Patel: I can run that — will do 2h with concurrency targets [24, 48, 72, 96] and max_batch_delay 15ms, measure mean/95th/99th and KV hit interplay.
[05:58] Priya Rao: please also include per-route breakdown so we can see which user flows suffer.
[06:03] Samir Patel: yes will add per-route breakdown and raw logs — note S3 link might be large.
[06:09] Jordan Lee: good. Aisha, can you remind us of the QPS target and latency SLO?
[06:15] Aisha Gomez: long term we want 550 qps at 95th <= 300ms for the main endpoint; short term for POC we'll accept 450 qps at 95th <= 350ms.
[06:27] Jordan Lee: noted — target 450 qps, 95th <=350ms for POC. We'll aim to hit that with config.
[06:33] Marcus Chen: question on routing: if we do sticky routing for cacheable sessions, how many users do we need to be sticky to make cache meaningful?
[06:41] Samir Patel: roughly if you can get 10-15% of traffic sticky with similar prefixes, you can boost overall hit rate materially. But depends on prefix overlap. I'll run simulation.
[06:51] Priya Rao: what about fallback policies? we want graceful degradation not hard failures.
[06:55] Samir Patel: Redwood supports model variant fallback — if primary model is overloaded we can route to smaller quantized variant and attach a small disclaimer. Also auto-failover to another region if needed. We configure percent of traffic to fallback during overload.
[07:07] Aisha Gomez: can we see cost delta for using a quantized variant for fallback?
[07:11] Jordan Lee: I'll include that in the cost estimate — approximate 30-40% lower GPU cost per token but some quality degradation.
[07:19] Marcus Chen: on the security side, our audits requested detailed logs for queueing and routing decisions. Do you have that in the demo?
[07:27] Samir Patel: yes we capture tracing hooks per request and per-decision logs — available in the console export; we can extend retention for Private/Dedicated.
[07:35] Priya Rao: perfect. Also, Marcus asked about SSO and RBAC for the POC console access.
[07:40] Jordan Lee: we already set up SAML SSO and role-based access for NimblePay team; Marcus you have admin rights, correct?
[07:46] Marcus Chen: yes I can see admin access.
[07:49] Aisha Gomez: one more thing — we noticed occasional transcription errors in the logs where model names get mangled, just FYI not urgent.
[07:56] Samir Patel: haha yeah we see that too, K-V cash sometimes shows up in logs — people type it wrong.
[08:02] Jordan Lee: alright let's recap the plan and action items. Samir will run the 2h stress with concurrency steps and batch delay 15ms, include per-route breakdown and KV hit analysis. Marcus will send SLOs and traffic shaping details. Jordan will send cost estimate and config recommendation. Priya will schedule the follow-up deep dive.
[08:20] Aisha Gomez: thanks all. Any blockers on Redwood side?
[08:24] Samir Patel: none. Will start runs tonight and post results tomorrow morning.
[08:29] Marcus Chen: we'll aim to be available for the follow-up.
[08:33] Jordan Lee: Perfect. We'll share the extended benchmark sheet and link to logs. Meeting adjourned.
[08:38] (end)
notes: Transcript contains typical ASR issues: some product names and acronyms may be incorrect; timestamps approximate. References: benchmark spreadsheet and deck uploaded to shared folder. Customer accepts follow-up deep dive next Tuesday.
